Margossian, Zhong and Mukherjee

Efficient Sampling for Ising and Potts Models
using Auxiliary Gaussian Variables

Charles C. Margossian* charles.margossian@ubc.ca Affiliation: Department of Statistics Affiliation: University of British Columbia Affiliation: Vancouver, BC, Canada    Chenyang Zhong* cz2755@columbia.edu Affiliation: Department of Statistics Affiliation: Columbia University Affiliation: New York, NY, USA    Sumit Mukherjee sm3949@columbia.edu Affiliation: Department of Statistics Affiliation: Columbia University Affiliation: New York, NY, USA Affiliation: *Equal contribution
Abstract

Ising and Potts models are an important class of discrete probability distributions which originated from statistical physics and since then have found applications in several disciplines. Simulation from these models is a well known challenging problem. In this paper, we study a class of Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms, in which we introduce an auxiliary Gaussian variable such that, conditional on this variable, the discrete states are independent. This approach is broadly applicable to Ising and Potts models, including ones in which the coupling matrix admits negative entries, as in spin glass and Hopfield models. We focus on a block Gibbs sampler version of this algorithm, which alternates between sampling the auxiliary Gaussian and the discrete states, and derive mixing time bounds for a wide class of Ising/Potts models at both high and low temperatures, yielding results analogous to those derived for the Heat Bath and Swendsen-Wang algorithms. We present novel choices of auxiliary Gaussian variables which scale well with the number of states in the Potts model, and which can take advantage of the low rank structure of the coupling matrix, if any. Finally, we numerically evaluate the performance of the auxiliary Gaussian Gibbs sampler with several competing algorithms, across a range of examples.

keywords
Ising models, Potts models, Markov chain Monte Carlo, Gibbs sampling, mixing time

1 Introduction

The Ising model is a probability distribution on the space of binary vectors of size nn, whose components are allowed to take two values, traditionally taken to be {0,1}\{0,1\} or {−1,1}\{-1,1\}. The Ising model was first introduced in statistical physics to study ferromagnetism (Ising, 1925). The Potts model (Potts, 1952) generalizes the Ising model to q≥2q\geq 2 states, where the states can be taken to be [q]:={1,2,⋯,q}[q]:=\{1,2,\cdots,q\}. With this choice, the Potts model is given by the following probability mass function on [q]n[q]^{n}:

ℙ(𝐗=𝐱)=1Z⁡(β,A)exp(β2∑i,j=1nAi​j1{xi=xj}).\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{Z(\beta,A)}\exp\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}A_{ij}1\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}\right). (1)

Here β>0\beta>0 is the inverse temperature parameter; the coupling matrix AA is a symmetric matrix which controls the dependence between the components of 𝐗{\bf X}, and Z⁡(β,A)Z(\beta,A) is the normalizing constant, also termed the partition function. We assume that the diagonal entries of AA equal 00, noting that this has no impact on the model (1). The most common choice of AA is as a scaled adjacency matrix of a graph on nn vertices. We consider both positive and negative entries for AA, thus covering both traditional Ising/Potts models and spin glass models under one framework.

Since their inception, the Ising and Potts models have found applications in a wide range of disciplines, including image processing, protein folding, neuroscience, and in the social sciences; see for example Lipowski (2022) and references therein. Two prominent cases of Ising models in machine learning are the Hopfield network and the Boltzmann machine (MacKay, 2003). One of the main reasons for the popularity of Ising and Potts models is that they are perhaps the simplest models which exhibit non-trivial dependence across their components.

Simulation plays a crucial role in understanding the properties of the Ising and Potts models, particularly through the computation of Monte Carlo estimators. Building efficient samplers for such models is a well-known challenge (Neal, 1993; Landau and Binder, 2009; Faulkner and Livingstone, 2024). Over the past decade, this problem has generated much interest in the machine learning community (Martens and Sutskever, 2010; Zhang et al., 2012; Pakman and Paninski, 2013; Grathwohl et al., 2021; Robnik et al., 2023, e.g). A general strategy, first proposed by Martens and Sutskever (2010), is to introduce an auxiliary Gaussian (AG) variable 𝐙{\bf Z}, such that the elements of 𝐗{\bf X} conditional on 𝐙{\bf Z} are mutually independent. It is then possible to construct Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms, which sample from the joint space (𝐗,𝐙)({\bf X},{\bf Z}). For example, we may implement a block Gibbs sampler that alternates between sampling from 𝐗|𝐙{\bf X}\mid{\bf Z} and 𝐙|𝐗{\bf Z}\mid{\bf X}. We refer to such an algorithm as an AG sampler. The idea of introducing a latent continuous variable to study discrete states in an Ising model can be further traced back to the Hubbard–Stratonovich transformation used in theoretical physics (Stratonovich, 1957; Hubbard, 1959).

The first contribution of our paper is algorithmic. We introduce two novel constructions of AG variables that in turn lead to new sampling algorithms. Specifically, we present a construction for Potts models and another construction for (approximately) low-rank coupling matrices AA, with applications to dense regular graphs and Hopfield networks. These constructions can be used separately or together.

The second contribution of our paper is theoretical and concerns bounds on the mixing time of the AG sampler. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first mixing time bounds for AG samplers. Such bounds exist for classical samplers, including the heat bath (Levin et al., 2010; Cuff et al., 2012, e.g.) and the Swendsen-Wang algorithm (Long et al., 2014; Gheissari et al., 2018; Galanis et al., 2019; Blanca et al., 2021, e.g.). The study of these bounds mainly focuses on cases where β\beta is small (high-temperature regime) and/or AA is the adjacency matrix of a complete graph (Curie-Weiss model). Our bounds demonstrate fast mixing of the AG sampler at high temperatures for a wide class of coupling matrices, including Ising and Potts models on graphs and spin glass models such as the Hopfield model. In some limited cases, such as the Curie-Weiss model, we also derive mixing bounds at low temperatures.

Finally, our paper contains extensive numerical experiments, which demonstrate the performance of AG samplers relative to existing algorithms. We examine a number of target distributions, including Potts models on graphs, Hopfield networks and spin glass models. We consider a range of temperatures, including settings where the system is near a critical temperature or cold. In many regimes, we find that the AG sampler yields the best performance.

2 Choices of Auxiliary Gaussian

In this section, we derive the auxiliary Gaussian algorithm for the Potts model. We then discuss a modification of the algorithm for low-rank coupling matrices AA that achieves higher computational efficiency.

2.1 Auxiliary Gaussian for Potts

In order to derive an auxiliary Gaussian variable for the Potts model, it is useful to rewrite the probability mass function in terms of one-hot variables. Consider a vector 𝐱=(x1,…,xn)∈[q]n{\mathbf{x}}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in[q]^{n}. For every ℓ∈[q]\ell\in[q], define the one-hot vector,

𝐲ℓ:=(1{x1=ℓ},…,1{xn=ℓ})′∈ℝn.{\mathbf{y}}_{\ell}:=(1\{x_{1}=\ell\},\ldots,1\{x_{n}=\ell\})^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

In other words, the ithi^{\text{th}} element of 𝐲ℓ\mathbf{y}_{\ell} is 1 if xi=ℓx_{i}=\ell, and 00 otherwise. This sets up a one-to-one map between 𝐱\mathbf{x} and (𝐲1,…,𝐲q)({\bf y}_{1},\ldots,{\bf y}_{q}). The log probability mass function of the Potts model may then be written as

β2∑i,j=1nAi​j1{xi=xj}=β2∑ℓ=1q𝐲ℓ′A𝐲ℓ,\frac{\beta}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}A_{ij}1\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}=\frac{\beta}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\mathbf{y}^{\prime}_{\ell}A\mathbf{y}_{\ell},

where the additive log normalizing constant has been dropped. The term 𝐲ℓ′​A​𝐲ℓ/2\mathbf{y}^{\prime}_{\ell}A\mathbf{y}_{\ell}/2 looks like the log moment generating function of a multivariate Gaussian, except that the matrix AA is not non-negative definite, as the diagonal entries of AA equal 00. Let λmin\lambda_{\text{min}} be the smallest eigenvalue of AA and consider λ\lambda such that λ>−λmin\lambda>-\lambda_{\text{min}}. We replace AA by A+λ​IA+\lambda I, where I∈ℝn×nI\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is the identity matrix, thus ensuring that A+λ​IA+\lambda I is positive definite. This change to the coupling matrix does not change the probability mass function. Indeed,

∑ℓ=1q𝐲ℓ′(A+λI)𝐲ℓ−∑ℓ=1q𝐲ℓ′A𝐲ℓ=λ∑ℓ=1q𝐲ℓ′𝐲ℓ=λ∑ℓ=1q∑i=1n1{xi=ℓ}=nλ,\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\mathbf{y}_{\ell}^{\prime}(A+\lambda I)\mathbf{y}_{\ell}-\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\mathbf{y}_{\ell}^{\prime}A\mathbf{y}_{\ell}=\lambda\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\mathbf{y}_{\ell}^{\prime}\mathbf{y}_{\ell}=\lambda\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\sum_{i=1}^{n}1\{x_{i}=\ell\}=n\lambda, (2)

where the last equality follows from the fact ∑ℓ=1q1{xi=ℓ}=1\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}1\{x_{i}=\ell\}=1 for each i∈[n]i\in[n], and the constant n​λn\lambda can be absorbed into the normalizing constant.

Setting

B:=β⁡(A+λ​I),B:=\beta(A+\lambda I), (3)

the marginal probability mass function of 𝐗\mathbf{X} can be written as

ℙ⁡(𝐗=𝐱)=1Z⁡(β,B)​exp⁡(12​∑ℓ=1q𝐲ℓ′​B​𝐲ℓ).\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{Z(\beta,B)}\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\mathbf{y}_{\ell}^{\prime}B\mathbf{y}_{\ell}\Big). (4)

We now introduce our auxiliary Gaussian variables. Given 𝐗=𝐱{\mathbf{X}}={\mathbf{x}}, let 𝐙1,…,𝐙q\mathbf{Z}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{Z}_{q} be mutually independent nn-dimensional Gaussian random vectors with

𝐙ℓ∼N⁡(𝐲ℓ,B−1).\displaystyle\mathbf{Z}_{\ell}\sim N\left(\mathbf{y}_{\ell},B^{-1}\right). (5)

Then one can check that given 𝐙:=(𝐙1,…,𝐙q){\mathbf{Z}}:=({\mathbf{Z}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbf{Z}}_{q}) the random variables (X1,…,Xn)(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}) are mutually independent, with

ℙ⁡(Xi=ℓ∣𝐙)=exp⁡(∑j=1nBi​j​zℓ​j)∑ℓ′=1qexp⁡(∑j=1nBi​j​zℓ′​j).\mathbb{P}(X_{i}=\ell\mid{\mathbf{Z}})=\frac{\exp\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}z_{\ell j}\right)}{\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{q}\exp\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}z_{\ell^{\prime}j}\right)}. (6)

By iterative sampling from (5) and (6), we obtain a block Gibbs sampler. This approach extends the block Gibbs sampler proposed by Martens and Sutskever (2010) for Ising models. We might also consider running MCMC directly over 𝐙{\bf Z} and then sampling 𝐗|𝐙{\bf X}\mid{\bf Z}. This is the strategy proposed by Zhang et al. (2012) for the Ising models. To do so, we need the unnormalized marginal density of 𝐙{\bf Z}, which is given by

p(𝐳1,⋯,𝐳q)∝exp(−12∑ℓ=1q𝐳ℓ′B𝐳ℓ)∏i=1n(∑ℓ=1qexp(∑j=1nBi​jzℓ​j)).\displaystyle p({{\bf z}_{1},\cdots,{\bf z}_{q}})\propto\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}{\mathbf{z}}_{\ell}^{\prime}B{\mathbf{z}}_{\ell}\Big)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\Big(\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\exp\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}z_{\ell j}\Big)\Big). (7)

The proofs of both (6) and (7) are in Appendix A.1.

2.2 Block Gibbs using an auxiliary Gaussian

In this section, we analyze the complexity of the block Gibbs sampler, obtained by alternating between (5) and (6). We refer to this algorithm as the AG sampler. Algorithm 1 provides details for the AG sampler. There and throughout the paper, we denote the tt​ht^{th} iteration of the Markov chain as 𝐱⁡(t){\bf x}(t). If we look at the jthj^{\text{th}} component, we write xj​(t)x_{j}(t).

The first conditional (5) requires sampling from a multivariate Gaussian distribution for each ℓ∈[q]\ell\in[q]. Each 𝐙ℓ{\bf Z}_{\ell} follows a Gaussian with the same covariance matrix BB and so the cost of sampling is dominated by the Cholesky decomposition and inversion of BB, an operation with complexity 𝒪⁡(n3)\mathcal{O}(n^{3}). However, BB remains unchanged between iterations, so the decomposition needs be done only once. Then, within each iteration, the cost is dominated by 2​q2q matrix-vector multiplications, each with cost 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}) (Algorithm 1 lines 9 and 11). Suppose we run MCMC for TT iterations. Then the complexity of the algorithm is 𝒪⁡(n3+T​n2​q)\mathcal{O}(n^{3}+Tn^{2}q). Provided n≪Tn\ll T, the cost of the initial Cholesky decomposition is marginal.

Remark 1.

Martens and Sutskever (2010) propose an auxiliary Gaussian variable over ℝq​n\mathbb{R}^{qn} for simulating Potts states. Plugging this choice into the AG sampler results in an algorithm with complexity 𝒪⁡(n3+T​n2​q2)\mathcal{O}(n^{3}+Tn^{2}q^{2}). By contrast, we propose using qq auxiliary Gaussian variables, each over ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, and the cost per iteration of our sampler scales linearly in qq, rather than quadratically.

2.3 State permutation step

The Potts model defined in (1) does not prefer any state ℓ∈[q]\ell\in[q] over another, and a permutation of the states does not change the probability mass. However, at cold temperatures, a Markov chain may take a long time to move from one configuration where a state ℓ\ell dominates to one where a state ℓ′\ell^{\prime} dominates. To remedy this issue, we may introduce a random permutation at each iteration τt\tau_{t} and do an update

xi​(t)←τt​(xi​(t)).x_{i}(t)\leftarrow\tau_{t}(x_{i}(t)). (8)

This update improves Monte Carlo estimates of quantities which vary under state permutations, for example the expected number of particles in a particular state ℓ\ell, 𝔼(∑i1{xi=ℓ})\mathbb{E}\left(\sum_{i}1\{x_{i}=\ell\}\right). However, it does not improve estimates of quantities invariant to these permutations, such as the system’s expected Hamiltonian, 𝔼(β∑i,jAi​j1{xi=xj}/2)\mathbb{E}\left(\beta\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}1\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}/2\right).

The permutation step is also a theoretical tool for bounding mixing times at cold temperatures because the bounded total variation distance accounts for functions which are sensitive to state permutations. In particular, the permutation step plays a role in Theorem 9, but it is not used to obtain bounds at high temperatures.

Remark 2.

It is possible to break the symmetry over states ℓ∈[q]\ell\in[q] by introducing a magnetic field in (1). Then (8) must be treated as a Metropolis proposal, accepted with probability min​[1,ℙ⁡(𝐗=τ⁡(x⁡(t)))/ℙ⁡(𝐗=x⁡(t))]\text{min}[1,\mathbb{P}({\bf X}=\tau(x(t)))/\mathbb{P}({\bf X}=x(t))], in order to preserve the correctness of the sampler. In the absence of a magnetic component, the acceptance probability is always 1.

2.4 Low-rank auxiliary Gaussian

For certain models, the modified coupling matrix BB, obtained after increasing the diagonal elements of AA, may be low-rank, either exactly or approximately. In this case, it is reasonable to believe that we don’t have to work with nn-dimensional Gaussian vectors but instead with a kk-dimensional Gaussian vector, where k=rank⁡(B)k={\rm rank}(B).

Such algorithms have already been explored in the setting of Ising models for the complete graph (Mukherjee et al., 2018), where

A=1n​𝟏𝟏′−1n​I,A=\frac{1}{n}{\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{\prime}-\frac{1}{n}I, (9)

has eigenvalues (1−1/n,−1/n,…,−1/n)(1-1/n,-1/n,\ldots,-1/n), where the multiplicity of the eigenvalue −1/n-1/n is n−1n-1. Even though rank⁡(A)=n{\rm rank}(A)=n in a strict sense, we can add I/nI/n to AA to get the matrix 𝟏𝟏′/n{\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{\prime}/n, which has eigenvalues (1,0,…,0)(1,0,\ldots,0), and rank 1. A similar approach was successful in analyzing the Ising model of a regular graph with degree ∝n\propto\sqrt{n} (Mukherjee and Xu, 2023), where rank⁡(A)∝n{\rm rank}(A)\propto\sqrt{n}.

To propose a general version of the low-rank algorithm, let B=β⁡(A+|λmin|​I)B=\beta(A+|\lambda_{\min}|I). Note it is sufficient to augment the diagonal elements with |λmin||\lambda_{\min}|, rather than λ>|λmin|\lambda>|\lambda_{\min}|. Let ∑i=1nμi​𝐩i​𝐩i′\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_{i}{\bf p}_{i}{\bf p}_{i}^{\prime} denote the spectral expansion of BB, where (μ1,…,μn)(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n}) are non-negative, and arranged in decreasing order, and 𝐩i∈ℝn\mathbf{p}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the eigenvector corresponding to eigenvalue μi\mu_{i}. Fixing ε>0\varepsilon>0, we introduce the low-rank approximation

B~=∑i:μi>εμi𝐩i𝐩i′.\tilde{B}=\sum_{i:\mu_{i}>\varepsilon}\mu_{i}\mathbf{p}_{i}\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\prime}. (10)

In other words, we treat the eigenvalues below ε\varepsilon as 0. Let k≤nk\leq n denote the rank of B~\tilde{B}, i.e. k:=∑i=1n1{μi>ε}k:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}1\{\mu_{i}>\varepsilon\}. Let ℚ\mathbb{Q} be the Potts model with BB replaced by B~\tilde{B}, i.e.

ℚ(𝐗=𝐱)=1Z⁡(β,B~)exp(12∑i,j=1nB~i​j1{xi=xj}).\displaystyle\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{Z(\beta,\tilde{B})}\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\tilde{B}_{ij}1\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}\right). (11)

The log unormalized probability mass ℚ\mathbb{Q} can be written as

12​∑ℓ=1q𝐲ℓ′​B~​𝐲ℓ=12​∑ℓ=1q∑j=1kμj​(𝐩j′​𝐲ℓ)2.\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\mathbf{y}_{\ell}^{\prime}\tilde{B}\mathbf{y}_{\ell}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}(\mathbf{p}_{j}^{\prime}\mathbf{y}_{\ell})^{2}. (12)

This representation motivates the following new auxiliary variable. Given 𝐗=𝐱\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}, let 𝐙:={Zℓ​j}ℓ∈[q],j∈[k]\mathbf{Z}:=\{Z_{\ell j}\}_{\ell\in[q],j\in[k]} be k​qkq mutually independent Gaussians with

Zℓ​j∼Normal​(𝐩j′​𝐲ℓ,1/μj).\displaystyle Z_{\ell j}\sim\text{Normal}(\mathbf{p}^{\prime}_{j}\mathbf{y}_{\ell},1/\mu_{j}). (13)

Then the conditional distribution of 𝐗{\mathbf{X}} given 𝐙{\mathbf{Z}} is

ℙ⁡(Xi=ℓ∣𝐙)=exp⁡(∑j=1kμj​zℓ​j​pj​i)∑ℓ′=1qexp⁡(∑j=1kμj​zℓ′​j​pj​i),\mathbb{P}(X_{i}=\ell\mid{\bf Z})=\frac{\exp\left(\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}z_{\ell j}p_{ji}\right)}{\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{q}\exp\left(\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}z_{\ell^{\prime}j}p_{ji}\right)}, (14)

which is straightforward to sample from. Also, the marginal density of 𝐙{\bf Z} has a similar low-rank structure and

p(𝐳)∝exp(−12∑ℓ=1q∑j=1kμjzℓ​j2)∏i=1n(∑ℓ=1qexp(∑j=1kμjzℓ​jpj​i))\displaystyle p(\mathbf{z})\propto\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}z_{\ell j}^{2}\Big)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\Big(\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\exp\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}z_{\ell j}p_{ji}\Big)\Big) (15)

The proof of both (14) and (15) are given in Appendix A.2.

By iterating between the steps (13) and (14), we again have a block Gibbs sampler. We no longer need to do an inversion and Cholesky decomposition but we do one Eigen decomposition instead, which incurs the same complexity 𝒪⁡(n3)\mathcal{O}(n^{3}). The cost per iteration is dominated by (i) calculating the mean of each univariate normal, that is doing q​kqk inner-products of nn-vectors in (13) and (ii) calculating the probability of sampling each state for each particle, which is q​nqn inner-products of kk-vectors in (14). Both operations have complexity 𝒪⁡(q​n​k)\mathcal{O}(qnk). The resulting Gibbs sampler with mm iterations has complexity 𝒪⁡(n3+T​q​n​k)\mathcal{O}(n^{3}+Tqnk). This is an improvement over the previously obtained complexity 𝒪⁡(n3+T​q​n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{3}+Tqn^{2}). In particular the improvement is significant when T≫n≫kT\gg n\gg k.

A tuning parameter when approximating AA as low-rank is the threshold ε\varepsilon, under which small eigenvalues of the coupling matrix are replaced by 0. To provide some guidance on setting ε\varepsilon, we bound the error on the low-rank AG sampler in the following proposition.

Proposition 3.

Let ℙ\mathbb{P} be the original Potts measure given in (4), and let ℚ\mathbb{Q} be the low-rank Potts measure given in (11). Then we have the following results:

  • (i) The difference in the log normalizing constant of the two models satisfies

    |log⁡Z⁡(β,B)−log⁡Z⁡(β,B~)|≤12​n​β​ε.|\log Z(\beta,B)-\log Z(\beta,\tilde{B})|\leq\frac{1}{2}n\beta\varepsilon.

  • (ii) With KL(.|.)\mathrm{KL}(.|.) denoting the Kullback-Leibler divergence between two probability measures, we have

    max⁡(KL⁡(ℙ|ℚ),KL⁡(ℚ|ℙ))≤n​β​ε.\max\Big(\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{P}|\mathbb{Q}),\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{Q}|\mathbb{P})\Big)\leq n\beta\varepsilon.

The proof is in Appendix A.3.

In general, the low-rank auxiliary Gaussian is useful when k=rank⁡(B~)≪nk={\rm rank}(\tilde{B})\ll n. The following proposition provides a simple sufficient condition as to when this happens.

Proposition 4.

Suppose λmax\lambda_{\max} and λmin\lambda_{\min} are the largest and smallest eigenvalues of AA. Let B:=β⁡(A+|λmin|​I)B:=\beta(A+|\lambda_{\min}|I), and B~\tilde{B} be its low-rank approximation for some ε>0\varepsilon>0. If

λmax=O⁡(1),λmin=o⁡(1),\displaystyle\lambda_{\max}=O(1),\quad\lambda_{\min}=o(1), (16)

then k:=rank⁡(B~)=o⁡(n)k:={\rm rank}(\tilde{B})=o(n).

The proof is in Appendix A.4.

The above lemma raises the question of whether there are natural examples of coupling matrices AA which satisfy (16). Below we give some examples of matrices AA which satisfy (16), and some examples which don’t. In cases where the Potts model is defined over a graph, we denote by A~\tilde{A} the adjacency matrix—noting that A∝A~A\propto\tilde{A}—and by dd the degree of a regular graph, that is the number of edges connected to each node.

  • •

    Satisfies (16): Ising model on the Complete Graph (Curie-Weiss model), random regular graphs and Erdős-Rényi graphs with large average degree, and certain Hopfield models:

    1. (a)

      Complete graphs. Here, all the nodes are connected to one another and A=1n​𝟏𝟏′−1n​IA=\frac{1}{n}{\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{\prime}-\frac{1}{n}I. Hence λmax=1−1n=O⁡(1)\lambda_{\max}=1-\frac{1}{n}=O(1) and λmin=−1n=o⁡(1)\lambda_{\min}=-\frac{1}{n}=o(1).

    2. (b)

      Random regular graphs. For d≤n/2d\leq n/\penalty 2 and A=A~/dA=\tilde{A}/d, we have λmax​(A~)=d\lambda_{\max}(\tilde{A})=d and λmin​(A~)=OP​(d)\lambda_{\min}(\tilde{A})=O_{P}(\sqrt{d}) (see Cook et al. (2018); Tikhomirov and Youssef (2019)). Consequently, as long as d→∞d\rightarrow\infty with n→∞n\to\infty, we have λmax=1=O⁡(1)\lambda_{\max}=1=O(1) and λmin=OP​(1/d)=oP​(1)\lambda_{\min}=O_{P}\big(1/\sqrt{d}\big)=o_{P}(1).

    3. (c)

      Erdös–Rényi graphs. For these graphs, we denote by pp the probability of there being an edge between two nodes. Then for p=d/np=d/n and A=A~/dA=\tilde{A}/d, we have that when d≫log⁡nd\gg\log n, then ‖A~−dn​𝟏𝟏′‖2=OP​(d)\big\|\tilde{A}-\frac{d}{n}{\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{\prime}\big\|_{2}=O_{P}(\sqrt{d}) (Benaych-Georges et al., 2020, Theorem 3.2). Hence ‖A−1n​𝟏𝟏′‖2=OP​(1/d)=oP​(1)\big\|A-\frac{1}{n}{\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{\prime}\big\|_{2}=O_{P}\big(1/\sqrt{d}\big)=o_{P}(1), and consequently λmax=1+oP​(1)=OP​(1),λmin=oP​(1)\lambda_{\max}=1+o_{P}(1)=O_{P}(1),\lambda_{\min}=o_{P}(1).

    4. (d)

      Hopfield models. The Hopfield model is defined by an m×nm\times n matrix 𝜼\bm{\eta} of i.i.d Rademacher random variables, i.e. P⁡(ηi​j=±1)=1/2P(\eta_{ij}=\pm 1)=1/2. The coupling matrix is then A=off-diag​(A~)A=\text{off-diag}(\widetilde{A}), where A~=𝜼′​𝜼/max⁡(m,n)\widetilde{A}=\bm{\eta}^{\prime}\bm{\eta}/\max(m,n). Note that A=A~−mmax⁡(m,n)​IA=\widetilde{A}-\frac{m}{\max(m,n)}I.

      When n≪mn\ll m, we have ‖A~−I‖2=‖1m​𝜼′​𝜼−I‖2=OP​(nm)=oP​(1)\|\widetilde{A}-I\|_{2}=\big\|\frac{1}{m}\bm{\eta}^{\prime}\bm{\eta}-I\big\|_{2}=O_{P}\big(\sqrt{\frac{n}{m}}\big)=o_{P}(1) (see (Vershynin, 2018, Theorem 4.7.1)). Consequently ‖A−𝟎‖2=oP​(1)\|A-{\bm{0}}\|_{2}=o_{P}(1), and so λmax=oP​(1),λmin=oP​(1)\lambda_{\max}=o_{P}(1),\lambda_{\min}=o_{P}(1).

      On the other hand, when m≪nm\ll n, we have A~=1n​𝜼′​𝜼\widetilde{A}=\frac{1}{n}{\bm{\eta}}^{\prime}{\bm{\eta}}, and in this regime (Vershynin, 2018, Theorem 4.7.1) gives 1n​𝜼​𝜼′≈pIm\frac{1}{n}{\bm{\eta}}{\bm{\eta}}^{\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\approx}}I_{m}. Since the nonzero eigenvalues of A~=1n​𝜼′​𝜼\widetilde{A}=\frac{1}{n}{\bm{\eta}}^{\prime}{\bm{\eta}} are the same as those of 1n​𝜼​𝜼′≈pIm\frac{1}{n}{\bm{\eta}}{\bm{\eta}}^{\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\approx}}I_{m}, we have λmax​(A~)=1+oP​(1)\lambda_{\max}(\widetilde{A})=1+o_{P}(1) and λmin​(A~)=oP​(1)\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde{A})=o_{P}(1). Consequently, λmax=λmax​(A~)−mn=1+oP​(1)\lambda_{\max}=\lambda_{\max}(\widetilde{A})-\frac{m}{n}=1+o_{P}(1) and λmin=λmin​(A~)−mn=oP​(1)\lambda_{\min}=\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde{A})-\frac{m}{n}=o_{P}(1).

      Note that the same applies if the components of 𝜼\bm{\eta} are σ2\sigma^{2}-sub-Gaussian random variables for a fixed σ\sigma. Thus the only case where the Hopfield model is not approximately low-rank is the regime when m∝nm\propto n.

  • •

    Does not satisfy (16): Ising model on graphs with bounded average (including Ising model on the dd dimensional integer lattice), Hopfield model with m=nm=n, and Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model.

If (16) is not satisfied, then it seems reasonable to prefer the regular version of the auxiliary Gaussian algorithm over the low-rank version. Numerical experiments suggest the regular version is faster when AA is full-rank.

2.5 Continuous relaxation of the Potts model

Rather than use a block Gibbs sampler which alternates between (𝐙∣𝐗)({\bf Z}\mid{\bf X}) and (𝐗∣𝐙)({\bf X}\mid{\bf Z}), it is possible to directly sample from p⁡(𝐙)p({\bf Z}) using (7) (or (15)), which gives the unnormalized marginal density of the matrix 𝐙{\mathbf{Z}}. The discrete states are then recovered by sampling from (𝐗∣𝐙)({\bf X}\mid{\bf Z}). This approach is particularly attractive, in that it lets us use gradient-based MCMC. For example, Zhang et al. (2012) use Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Neal, 2011; Betancourt, 2018, HMC;) to sample over the marginal distribution of 𝐙{\bf Z} for the Ising model. Their strategy can be applied to Potts models and/or models with a low-rank coupling matrix AA, using the auxiliary Gaussian variables we propose.

One difficulty is that p⁡(𝐙)p({\bf Z}) is highly multimodal, especially for large β\beta, which can lead to long mixing times, even with gradient-based MCMC. Furthermore, HMC is difficult to tune, and self-tuning strategies, such as the No-U Turn Sampler (Hoffman and Gelman, 2014, NUTS;) are not straightforward to implement; a similar observation is made by Grathwohl et al. (2021). In our numerical experiments, we consider an HMC algorithm using the proposed AG variables; however, the tuning parameters are held fixed and are likely suboptimal. Finding a well-tuned gradient-based sampler for p⁡(𝐙)p({\bf Z}) is left as an open problem.

3 Theoretical Analysis of Mixing Time

Monte Carlo estimators generated by MCMC suffer from a non-asymptotic bias, due to MCMC’s biased initialization, i.e. 𝐱⁡(0)\mathbf{x}(0) is not drawn from (1). Hence, we need to overcome this initial bias during a burn-in phase before accumulating samples to construct our Monte Carlo estimators. A common metric to quantify the number of necessary burn-in iterations is the total variation mixing time, which can be used to bound the bias of Monte Carlo estimators over discrete spaces (Sinclair, 1993; Diaconis, 2009; Levin and Peres, 2017; Dwivedi et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020, e.g.). In this section, we present theoretical results on the mixing time of the AG sampler introduced in the previous section. The proofs of our theoretical results are deferred to Sections 5 and 6.

We first review total variation mixing time. Let ℕ\mathbb{N} be the natural numbers and ℕ∗\mathbb{N}^{*} the natural numbers excluding 00. Consider a Markov chain X⁡(t)X(t) with t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N} on a finite state space Ω\Omega, and let π\pi denote the chain’s stationary distribution. For any x0∈Ωx_{0}\in\Omega and t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}, we denote by Kx0tK^{t}_{x_{0}} the distribution of X⁡(t)X(t) for a chain initialized at X⁡(0)=x0X(0)=x_{0}. The total variation distance between Kx0tK_{x_{0}}^{t} and π\pi is defined as

‖Kx0t−π‖TV:=12​∑x∈Ω|Kx0t​(x)−π⁡(x)|,\|K_{x_{0}}^{t}-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x\in\Omega}|K_{x_{0}}^{t}(x)-\pi(x)|,

and takes values over [0,1][0,1]. Standard theory of finite Markov chains guarantees that the total variation distance converges to 0 as t→∞t\to\infty under irreducibility and aperiodicity (Neal, 1993; Levin and Peres, 2017, e.g.). Unfortunately, this asymptotic result tells us little about the behavior of Markov chains over a finite number of iterations.

To better understand the pre-asymptotic behavior of MCMC, we study the ϵ\epsilon-mixing time. Let d⁡(t):=maxx0∈Ω⁡‖Kx0t−π‖TVd(t):=\max_{x_{0}\in\Omega}\|K_{x_{0}}^{t}-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}. For any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, the ϵ\epsilon-mixing time is defined as

tmix​(ϵ):=min⁡{t∈ℕ:d⁡(t)≤ϵ}.t_{\mathrm{mix}}(\epsilon):=\min\{t\in\mathbb{N}:d(t)\leq\epsilon\}.

Bounding d⁡(t)d(t) ensures that the result holds for any choice of initialization.

We now take X⁡(t)X(t) to be the ttht^{\text{th}} sample generated by the AG sampler, and so Ω=[q]n\Omega=[q]^{n} and π\pi is the probability mass function in (1). To use the AG sampler, we need to construct a modified coupling matrix, B=β⁡(A+λ​I)B=\beta(A+\lambda I), for some λ>|λmin|\lambda>|\lambda_{\text{min}}|, where we recall that λmin\lambda_{\text{min}} is the smallest eigenvalue of AA. Any choice of λ\lambda produces a correct Gibbs sampler, however for a small λ\lambda we will obtain stronger guarantees on mixing time. These guarantees are mediated by the 1-norm of BB,

‖B‖1:=max⁡∑i=1nj∈[n]⁡|Bi​j|,\|B\|_{1}:=\max_{j\in[n]}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|B_{ij}|, (17)

which for a fixed AA is minimized for a small λ\lambda.

Theorem 5.

Assume that ‖B‖1<4/q\|B\|_{1}<4/\penalty q. For any ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1), the ϵ\epsilon-mixing time of the AG sampler satisfies

tmix​(ϵ)≤⌈log⁡ϵ−1+log⁡n−log⁡(q​‖B‖1/4)⌉.t_{\mathrm{mix}}(\epsilon)\leq\left\lceil\frac{\log{\epsilon^{-1}}+\log{n}}{-\log\big(q\|B\|_{1}/\penalty 4\big)}\right\rceil.
Remark 6.

Theorem 5 applies to the Curie-Weiss model (Potts model on the complete graph, with the coupling matrix given by (9); see Section 4.2.2 for details), Potts models on lattice graphs (see Section 4.2.1), and the Hopfield model:

  • •

    For the Curie-Weiss model, we can take λ\lambda slightly larger than n−1n^{-1}. In this case, ‖B‖1=β\|B\|_{1}=\beta and our result implies that the AG sampler is fast mixing for β∈(0,4/q)\beta\in(0,4/\penalty q). When q=2q=2 (corresponding to the mean-field Ising model), this range covers the entire high temperature regime.

  • •

    For the Potts model on a lattice graph in ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d}, we can take AA to be the adjacency matrix of the graph normalized by 2​d2d. In this case, |λmin|≤‖A‖1≤1|\lambda_{\min}|\leq\|A\|_{1}\leq 1 and any choice of λ>1\lambda>1 suffices. As ‖B‖1≤β⁡(‖A‖1+λ)≤β⁡(1+λ)\|B\|_{1}\leq\beta(\|A\|_{1}+\lambda)\leq\beta(1+\lambda), our result implies that the AG sampler is fast mixing for β∈(0,2/q)\beta\in(0,2/\penalty q). In fact, the same calculation shows that the AG sampler is fast mixing in the above regime when AA is the (scaled) adjacency matrix of any dnd_{n}-regular graph, where dnd_{n} can be fixed or grow with nn at an arbitrary rate.

  • •

    For the Hopfield model with m≫n2​log⁡nm\gg n^{2}\log n, take A=off-diag​(A~)A=\text{off-diag}(\widetilde{A}) with A~=𝜼′​𝜼/max⁡(m,n)\widetilde{A}=\bm{\eta}^{\prime}\bm{\eta}/\max(m,n). Standard concentration bounds for sub-exponential random variables (see e.g. (Vershynin, 2018, Corollary 2.8.3)) and a union bound yield that

    ∥A∥1=maxj∈[n]∑i∈[n]:i≠j|∑k=1mηk​iηk​j|max⁡(m,n)=𝒪(n​m​log⁡nm)=o(1)\|A\|_{1}=\frac{\max_{j\in[n]}\sum_{i\in[n]:i\neq j}\big|\sum_{k=1}^{m}\eta_{ki}\eta_{kj}\big|}{\max(m,n)}=\mathcal{O}\bigg(\frac{n\sqrt{m\log{n}}}{m}\bigg)=o(1)

    with high probability. Hence the AG sampler is fast mixing.

Remark 7.

The mixing time upper bound in Theorem 5 increases with ‖B‖1\|B\|_{1}. As ‖B‖1\|B\|_{1} increases with λ>|λmin|\lambda>|\lambda_{\text{min}}|, our result provides a theoretical justification for choosing λ\lambda to be only slightly larger than |λmin||\lambda_{\min}|. This formalizes an empirical observation made by Martens and Sutskever (2010) that a small λ\lambda yields better performance.

Without the high temperature restriction, the mixing time can be at most exponential in n​‖B‖1n\|B\|_{1}, as shown in Theorem 8 below.

Theorem 8.

For any ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1), the ϵ\epsilon-mixing time of the AG sampler satisfies

tmix​(ϵ)≤⌈exp⁡(2​‖B‖1​n)​log⁡(ϵ−1)⌉.t_{\mathrm{mix}}(\epsilon)\leq\lceil\exp(2\|B\|_{1}n)\log(\epsilon^{-1})\rceil.

Theorem 8 gives a bound on the worst case mixing time, and it is very much possible to have faster mixing for particular models, even at low temperatures.

To show this, we consider the low-rank AG sampler (Section 2.4) with a permutation step (Section 2.3). Theorem 9 shows that for the Curie-Weiss model (Potts model on the complete graph, with coupling matrix (9)), the AG sampler mixes within 𝒪⁡(log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(\log{n}) iterations, even in the low temperature regime.

Theorem 9.

Consider the Curie-Weiss model with q≥2q\geq 2, and assume that the inverse temperature β>q\beta>q. For any ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1), the ϵ\epsilon-mixing time of the modified AG sampler described as above satisfies

tmix​(ϵ)≤C​log⁡(n+1)​⌈log⁡(ϵ−1)⌉,t_{\mathrm{mix}}(\epsilon)\leq C\log(n+1)\lceil\log(\epsilon^{-1})\rceil,

where CC only depends on q,βq,\beta.

Remark 10.

For the Curie-Weiss model with general qq, there are three critical temperatures βu≤βo≤βr​c=q\beta_{u}\leq\beta_{o}\leq\beta_{rc}=q. Following Galanis et al. (2019), βu\beta_{u} corresponds to the uniqueness/non-uniqueness threshold, βo\beta_{o} corresponds to the ordered/disordered phase transition, and βr​c\beta_{rc} was conjectured to correspond to a second uniqueness/non-uniqueness threshold (Häggström (1996)); see Costeniuc et al. (2005); Cuff et al. (2012); Galanis et al. (2016) for further details. When β∈(βu,βr​c)\beta\in(\beta_{u},\beta_{rc}), the Curie-Weiss model exhibits metastable behavior and we expect common MCMC samplers to be slow mixing in this regime (see e.g. Galanis et al. (2019); Coja-Oghlan et al. (2023)). Theorem 9 implies fast mixing of the modified AG sampler for the Curie-Weiss model throughout the low temperature regime β>βr​c\beta>\beta_{rc}.

4 Numerical Experiments

In this section, we numerically evaluate the performance of the AG sampler across a range of Ising and Potts models. The code to reproduce the experiments and figures can be found at https://github.com/charlesm93/potts_simulation.

As benchmarks, we consider several MCMC algorithms. An important class of algorithms are Metropolis algorithms, which propose a new state 𝐱′{\bf x}^{\prime} and accept it with a certain probability. Specifically, we consider Barker’s acceptance rule, which is to accept the proposed state with probability,

α=ℙ⁡(𝐱′)ℙ⁡(𝐱)+ℙ⁡(𝐱′)=11+eℒ⁡(𝐱)−ℒ⁡(𝐱′),\alpha=\frac{\mathbb{P}({\bf x}^{\prime})}{\mathbb{P}({\bf x})+\mathbb{P}({\bf x}^{\prime})}=\frac{1}{1+e^{\mathcal{L}({\bf x})-\mathcal{L}({\bf x}^{\prime})}}, (18)

where ℒ⁡(𝐱):=log⁡ℙ⁡(𝐱)\mathcal{L}({\bf x}):=\log\mathbb{P}({\bf x}). In the special case where q=2q=2 and the proposal is obtained by “flipping” a single element xix_{i}, an iteration of the Metropolis algorithm with Barker’s acceptance rule is exactly one iteration of the heat bath algorithm or Gibbs sampler, which draws a new state from the conditional distribution ℙ⁡(Xi∣𝐱−i)\mathbb{P}(X_{i}\mid{\bf x}_{-i}). A crucial choice in the Metropolis algorithm is to determine which site ii to update. This can be done by sampling ii uniformly from [n][n] at each iteration, using a schedule that sequentially updates each site, or with a more sophisticated proposal as in Gibbs-with-Gradient (Grathwohl et al., 2021). The calculation of ℒ⁡(𝐱)−ℒ⁡(𝐱′)\mathcal{L}({\bf x})-\mathcal{L}({\bf x}^{\prime}) can be done by treating ℒ⁡(𝐱)\mathcal{L}({\bf x}) as a user-provided black box function with computational cost 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}). However, if the difference between 𝐱{\bf x} and 𝐱′{\bf x}^{\prime} is only one element, then ℒ⁡(𝐱)−ℒ⁡(𝐱′)\mathcal{L}({\bf x})-\mathcal{L}({\bf x}^{\prime}) can be computed in 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) operations, given an initial calculation of ℙ⁡(𝐱)\mathbb{P}({\bf x}) at the first iteration of MCMC. All the Metropolis algorithms we consider update a single site and so, unless otherwise specified, we use the specialized calculation of ℒ⁡(𝐱)−ℒ⁡(𝐱′)\mathcal{L}({\bf x})-\mathcal{L}({\bf x}^{\prime}).

We also consider the Wolff algorithm (Wolff, 1989) for Potts models defined on graphs. The Wolff algorithm is similar to the Swendsen-Wang algorithm but only updates a single cluster per iteration. In preliminary runs, we found that the Wolff algorithm consistently outperforms the Swendsen-Wang algorithm and so we only report results for the Wolff algorithm.

Finally, we examine three samplers which use an auxiliary Gaussian variable: the AG sampler, the AG sampler with a low-rank auxiliary Gaussian, and discrete Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. The algorithms we evaluate are summarized in Table 1.

4.1 Performance metric

A typical goal with MCMC is to estimate expectation values, that is, for a function ϕ:[q]n→Φ⊆ℝ\phi:[q]^{n}\to\Phi\subseteq\mathbb{R}, we estimate 𝔼⁡[ϕ⁡(𝐗)]\mathbb{E}\left[\phi(\mathbf{X})\right]. Our estimator is

ϕ^T=1⌈T/2⌉​∑t=⌈T/2⌉Tϕ⁡(𝐱(t)),\hat{\phi}_{T}=\frac{1}{\lceil T/2\rceil}\sum^{T}_{t=\lceil T/2\rceil}\phi\left(\mathbf{x}^{(t)}\right), (19)

where (𝐱⁡(0),⋯,𝐱⁡(T))(\mathbf{x}(0),\cdots,\mathbf{x}(T)) are samples obtained via MCMC and TT is the total number of iterations. Following Gelman and Shirley (2011), we discard the first half of the Markov chain as part of a burn-in phase. As a quantity of interest, we focus on ϕ(𝐱)=−∑i,j=1nAi​j1{xi=xj}\phi({\bf x})=-\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}A_{ij}1\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}, which is the system’s Hamiltonian and is a sufficient statistics of (1).

We compute two statistics to evaluate the quality of ϕ^T\hat{\phi}_{T}:

  • (i)

    The R^\widehat{R}-statistics (Gelman and Rubin, 1992; Vehtari et al., 2020), which compares the mean of multiple chains initialized at distinct points and approaches 1 as the Markov chain converges.

  • (ii)

    The effective sample size (ESS), which for TT large enough can be interpreted as the number of independent samples required to achieve the variance of ϕ^T\hat{\phi}_{T} (Roberts and Rosenthal, 2004). Following the recommendation of Vehtari et al. (2020), we will use the ESS to characterize the error of ϕ^T\hat{\phi}_{T}, provided R^≈1\widehat{R}\approx 1.

We compute both quantities using the R package Posterior (Buerkner et al., 2020).

Our goal is to achieve convergence and a target ESS in as short a time as possible. There is no basic operations common to all the algorithms we consider, so the computational cost of a sampler is measured by its runtime (wall time). This means that our results depend on the implementation details of each algorithm. For this experiment, all samplers are implemented in R. For each algorithm, we run 4 chains in order to compute R^\widehat{R}. For the AG sampler, each chain is made of 50,000 iterations. The length of the chains for other algorithms is roughly set to keep total runtimes between methods comparable.

4.2 Potts models on a graph

We begin with the case where AA is the adjacency matrix of a graph GG scaled by its average degree. We consider two choices of GG which are of wide interest in statistical physics: the Ising model on the integer lattice and the Curie-Weiss model.

4.2.1 Lattice graph

The two-dimensional lattice graph with two states (i.e. q=2q=2) is possibly the best studied example. We examine a 24×2424\times 24 graph (i.e. n=576n=576), and consider the cases q=2,4q=2,4. We focus on a parameter range in β\beta around the critical temperature βc​(q)\beta_{c}(q), which is approximately 0.710.71 and 0.550.55 for q=2q=2 and q=4q=4 respectively, as reported by Monroe (2002). For q=2q=2, we illustrate the use of R^\widehat{R} (Figure 1). We find that all algorithms achieve R^≲1.1\widehat{R}\lesssim 1.1, which suggests approximate convergence (a more conservative threshold would be 1.01), and so calculations of the ESS provide a reasonable characterization of the Monte Carlo estimator’s error. We find that R^\widehat{R} decays fastest for the AG sampler. On the other hand, HMC struggles to converge and we attribute this to the difficulty of finding suitable tuning parameters which work well when sampling from p⁡(𝐙)p({\bf Z}).

Figure 2 plots the ESS/s for q=2q=2 and q=4q=4. In both cases, the AG sampler offers the best performance. The results also highlight important variations between different Metropolis algorithms. The black box Metropolis performs poorly but we see a net improvement when using a specialized calculation of ℒ⁡(𝐱′)−ℒ⁡(𝐱)\mathcal{L}({\bf x}^{\prime})-\mathcal{L}({\bf x}). Gibbs-with-gradient performs well for q=2q=2 but the performance decreases for q=4q=4; we attribute this to the increased cost of computing a gradient-based proposal for Potts models. Overall Metropolis Long, which updates the sites in sequence, produces the best performance among Metropolis algorithms. More sophisticated strategies, such as the Wolff algorithm provide better ESS per iteration but this does not justify the high wall time cost per iteration. We highlight that our implementation of Wolff does not exploit the sparsity of AA and that discrete HMC used static (and likely suboptimal) tuning parameters.11 1 Pilot runs with the self-tuning HMC implemented in Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017) also did not produce convincing results.

4.2.2 Curie-Weiss model

In this model An=𝟏𝟏′/n−In/nA_{n}={\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{\prime}/n-I_{n}/n is the scaled adjacency matrix of a complete graph, where each node is connected to every other node. Once again, we consider the cases q=2,4q=2,4 with n=576n=576. The critical value βc​(q)\beta_{c}(q) is 11 and ∼\sim1.64 for q=2q=2 and q=4q=4 respectively (Bollobás et al., 1996, e.g), around which we focus our simulations. Adjusting the diagonal elements, we obtain a rank-1 coupling matrix on which we can apply the low-rank AG variable.

For q=2q=2, the results are consistent with what we observed on the grid model, with the AG sampler producing the most competitive results (Figure 3). Using a low-rank AG offers a dramatic improvement, as might be expected, since for a fully-connected graph, the dimension of the auxiliary Gaussian variables can be reduced from n=576n=576 to k=1k=1. All algorithms suffer from an observable slow-down at the critical temperature, βc=1\beta_{c}=1.

Similarly for q=4q=4 (Figure 3), we observe a critical slow down near β≈1.65\beta\approx 1.65. Away from this point, the performance of all samplers improves, including at cold temperatures (β≥q\beta\geq q). Theorems 5 and 9 predict fast mixing times for the AG algorithms when β∉(1,4)\beta\notin(1,4). The experiment reveals that AG samplers can also perform well within β∈(1,4)\beta\in(1,4), and that the exponential bound by Theorem 8 is conservative. Finally, we note that the critical slow down around β≈1.65\beta\approx 1.65 has been analyzed in previous studies on the heat bath (Cuff et al., 2012); empirically we find this result to generalize to AG samplers.

4.3 Spin glass models

In a spin glass model, the entries in AA can take both positive and negative values. Two important examples are the Hopfield model and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) model. For these problems, auxiliary cluster algorithms, including the Wolff and Swendsen-Wang algorithms, are no longer an option. Moving forward, we only use Metropolis Long (with sequential updates) as a benchmark.

4.3.1 Hopfield Model

Let 𝜼∈ℝm×n\bm{\eta}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} be a matrix of i.i.d random variables with P⁡(ηi​k=±1)=1/2P(\eta_{ik}=\pm 1)=1/2, and let

A=𝜼′​𝜼max⁡(m,n).\displaystyle A=\frac{\bm{\eta}^{\prime}\bm{\eta}}{\max(m,n)}. (20)

AA can take values which are positive, negative, or zero, meaning the spins XiX_{i} can be correlated, anti-correlated, or uncorrelated.

We use this example to examine the validity of the above prediction, and to compare the regular and the low-rank AG samplers across varying ranks. We set β=1\beta=1, q=4q=4, n=576n=576, and vary mm from 1 to 200. We plot the results in Figure 4, and find AG samplers to outperform the Metropolis sampler, with the low-rank AG yielding a large improvement for small mm.

Remark 11.

In all our experiments, the regular and low-rank AG generate roughly the same effective sample size. The difference in performance is therefore driven by the difference in the computational cost of each iteration.

4.3.2 Cold SK model

In the SK model, the elements of a coupling matrix Ai​jA_{ij} are mutually independent, drawn from a standard normal scaled by 1/n1/\sqrt{n}, equivalently a normal with variance 1/n1/n:

Ai​j=Aj​i∼Normal​(0,n−1).A_{ij}=A_{ji}\sim\text{Normal}\left(0,n^{-1}\right).

This coupling matrix unfortunately does not admit a good low-rank approximation (c.f. Basak and Mukherjee (2017, Sec 1.3.2)). An important application of this model in physics is the study of spin glass systems at cold temperatures (Yucesoy, 2013; Katzgraber et al., 2001, e.g). For high β\beta, the Potts model becomes highly multimodal, resulting in a slow or incomplete exploration by the Markov chains.

Parallel tempering can mitigate this problem (Geyer, 1991; Hukushima et al., 1998); see also Swendsen and Wang (1986) for an earlier related proposal. Parallel tempering runs multiple chains or replicas over a schedule of temperatures for a set number of iterations and then exchanges, with a certain probability, the states of two replicas with a “neighboring” temperature. The probability of exchanging two neighboring replicas is chosen so as to maintain detailed balance. At high temperatures, the Markov chain can move more easily across the target space and overcome the energy barriers between modes, before being cooled down again to sample at the temperature of interest.

When implementing a tempering algorithm, we need to choose the number of replicas and their respective temperatures. The first replica is at the cold temperature of interest. We then progressively increase the temperature of each replica to ensure that the exchange probability is high and that we eventually reach a warm temperature at which the sampler is not frustrated by high energy barriers. In our experiment, the target inverse-temperature is β=3\beta=3. We create 11 replicas at evenly spaced temperatures, β=(0.5,0.75,1,1.25,1.5,1.75,2,2.25,2.5,2.75,3)\beta=(0.5,0.75,1,1.25,1.5,1.75,2,2.25,2.5,2.75,3). This naive approach yields reasonable, if somewhat uneven, acceptance rates for the exchange proposals. There is extensive literature on setting the temperature schedule for parallel tempering using more principled, albeit more intricate, approaches (Syed et al., 2022; Atchadé et al., 2011; Kone and Kofke, 2005; Hukushima et al., 1998, e.g.) and we leave the analysis of such tempering strategies with AG sampler to future work.

In total, we attempt 40 exchanges and run 2,000 iterations between exchanges, for a total of 80,000 iterations. We run 4 sets of replicas with different initializations to compute R^\widehat{R} and monitor whether the chains are mixing. The size of the system is n=128n=128.

We plot the results of our experiment in Figure 5. The non-tempered AG suffers at cold temperatures, notably for β≥2.5\beta\geq 2.5. The tempered AG is competitive across all temperature regimes, matching the superiority of the regular AG sampler for small β\betas, and yielding reasonable results for β\beta large. However, we did not find that AG methods outperform the tempered Metropolis sampler for β≥2\beta\geq 2.

5 Proofs of Theorems 5 and 8

In this section, we present the proofs of Theorems 5 and 8 in Sections 5.1 and 5.2, respectively. For any 𝐱=(x1,⋯,xn),𝐱′=(x1′,⋯,xn′)∈[q]n\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n}),\mathbf{x}^{\prime}=(x_{1}^{\prime},\cdots,x_{n}^{\prime})\in[q]^{n}, we denote the Hamming distance between 𝐱\mathbf{x} and 𝐱′\mathbf{x}^{\prime} by H(𝐱,𝐱′):=∑i=1n1{xi≠xi′}H(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}1\{x_{i}\neq x_{i}^{\prime}\}.

The proof of Theorem 5 is based on the path coupling technique (Levin and Peres, 2017, Chapter 14). To apply this technique, we associate a labeled undirected graph with vertex set [q]n[q]^{n}, so that any two states 𝐱=(x1,⋯,xn),𝐱′=(x1′,⋯,xn′)∈[q]n\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n}),\mathbf{x}^{\prime}=(x_{1}^{\prime},\cdots,x_{n}^{\prime})\in[q]^{n} are connected by an edge if and only if H⁡(𝐱,𝐱′)=1H(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=1.

In the following, we consider any two distinct states 𝐱=(x1,⋯,xn),𝐱′=(x1′,⋯,xn′)∈[q]n\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n}),\mathbf{x}^{\prime}=(x_{1}^{\prime},\cdots,x_{n}^{\prime})\in[q]^{n}. We aim to construct a coupling of 𝐗⁡(1)\mathbf{X}(1) and 𝐗′​(1)\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(1) such that 𝔼⁡[H⁡(𝐗⁡(1),𝐗′​(1))]\mathbb{E}[H(\mathbf{X}(1),\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(1))] is small.

6 Proof of Theorem 9

In this section, we present the proof of Theorem 9. We assume β>q\beta>q throughout this section. For any 𝐱=(x1,⋯,xn)∈[q]n\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n})\in[q]^{n}, we define C⁡(𝐱):=(C1​(𝐱),⋯,Cq​(𝐱))C(\mathbf{x}):=(C_{1}(\mathbf{x}),\cdots,C_{q}(\mathbf{x})), where for each ℓ∈[q]\ell\in[q], Cℓ​(𝐱):=n−1​∑i=1n𝟙xi=ℓC_{\ell}(\mathbf{x}):=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbbm{1}_{x_{i}=\ell} is the proportion of color ℓ\ell in 𝐱\mathbf{x}.

Our proof of Theorem 9 consists of four main steps. Firstly, we show the convergence of a deterministic iteration in Section 6.2. Then we show in Proposition 22 that within 𝒪⁡(log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(\log{n}) iterations, there is a color whose proportion is greater than the proportion of any other color by a constant amount. Based on this, we show in Proposition 23 that the state evolution of the AG sampler is closely approximated by this deterministic iteration and, as a result, the macroscopic proportions of the qq colors are close to the expected proportions. Finally, after the macroscopic proportions of all colors have converged, we develop a novel coupling argument to show that the AG sampler mixes in 𝒪⁡(log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(\log{n}) iterations in Section 6.4.

6.1 Notations and preliminary lemmas

In this subsection, we present some notations and preliminary lemmas that will be used in later parts of the proof. We start with the following two definitions.

Definition 12.

We define 𝒳:={𝛂=(α1,⋯,αq):α1,⋯,αq≥0,∑ℓ=1qαℓ=1}\mathcal{X}:=\big\{\bm{\alpha}=(\alpha_{1},\cdots,\alpha_{q}):\alpha_{1},\cdots,\alpha_{q}\geq 0,\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\alpha_{\ell}=1\big\}. For any ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0, we define 𝒳ε:={𝛂=(α1,⋯,αq)∈𝒳:α1≥⋯≥αq,α1−α2≥ε}\mathcal{X}_{\varepsilon}:=\{\bm{\alpha}=(\alpha_{1},\cdots,\alpha_{q})\in\mathcal{X}:\alpha_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\alpha_{q},\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}\geq\varepsilon\}. For any 𝛂=(α1,⋯,αq)∈ℝq\bm{\alpha}=(\alpha_{1},\cdots,\alpha_{q})\in\mathbb{R}^{q}, we define Φ⁡(𝛂):=(Φ1​(𝛂),Φ2​(𝛂),⋯,Φq​(𝛂))\Phi(\bm{\alpha}):=(\Phi_{1}(\bm{\alpha}),\Phi_{2}(\bm{\alpha}),\cdots,\Phi_{q}(\bm{\alpha})) with

Φℓ​(𝜶):=eβ​αℓ∑s=1qeβ​αs=Tℓ​(β​α1,β​α2,⋯,β​αq), for every ​ℓ∈[q],\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha}):=\frac{e^{\beta\alpha_{\ell}}}{\sum_{s=1}^{q}e^{\beta\alpha_{s}}}=T_{\ell}(\beta\alpha_{1},\beta\alpha_{2},\cdots,\beta\alpha_{q}),\text{ for every }\ell\in[q],

where TℓT_{\ell} is as in (24).

Assume that β>q\beta>q. Then the following conclusions hold:

For any 𝛂,𝛂′∈ℝq\bm{\alpha},\bm{\alpha}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{q}, we have ‖Φ⁡(𝛂′)−Φ⁡(𝛂)‖1≤2​β​q​‖𝛂′−𝛂‖∞\|\Phi(\bm{\alpha}^{\prime})-\Phi(\bm{\alpha})\|_{1}\leq 2\beta q\|\bm{\alpha^{\prime}}-\bm{\alpha}\|_{\infty}.

There exist positive constants ρ0,δ0∈(0,1)\rho_{0},\delta_{0}\in(0,1) that only depend on q,βq,\beta, such that for any 𝛂=(α1,⋯,αq),𝛂′=(α1′,⋯,αq′)∈ℝq\bm{\alpha}=(\alpha_{1},\cdots,\alpha_{q}),\bm{\alpha}^{\prime}=(\alpha^{\prime}_{1},\cdots,\alpha^{\prime}_{q})\in\mathbb{R}^{q} with max⁡{‖𝛂−𝛂0‖2,‖𝛂′−𝛂0‖2}≤δ0\max\{\|\bm{\alpha}-\bm{\alpha}_{0}\|_{2},\|\bm{\alpha}^{\prime}-\bm{\alpha}_{0}\|_{2}\}\leq\delta_{0} and ∑ℓ=1qαℓ=∑ℓ=1qαℓ′\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\alpha_{\ell}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\alpha_{\ell}^{\prime}, we have ‖Φ⁡(𝛂′)−Φ⁡(𝛂)‖1≤ρ0​‖𝛂′−𝛂‖1\|\Phi(\bm{\alpha}^{\prime})-\Phi(\bm{\alpha})\|_{1}\leq\rho_{0}\|\bm{\alpha}^{\prime}-\bm{\alpha}\|_{1}.

In this subsection, we introduce the following convenient notation. 7 Discussion

This paper builds on a growing literature on sampling methods for Ising and Potts models, using an auxiliary Gaussian variable, a strategy first proposed in the machine learning literature by Martens and Sutskever (2010). We present two novel choices of auxiliary Gaussian variables: (i) a choice for Potts models, which leads to a sampler whose cost per iteration scales linearly in qq; and (ii) a choice which automatically detects the (approximately) low-rank structure of 𝐀\bf A and takes advantage of this low-rank structure, if it exists. We primarily focus on the AG sampler, which is a block Gibbs sampler. We run an extensive suite of numerical experiments and identify many regimes where the AG sampler outperforms competitors, at times yielding an ESS/s which is orders of magnitudes higher—for example for Ising models on a graph and low-rank Hopfield networks. We also identify regimes where the AG sampler exhibits poor performance, for example when applied to a cold spin glass system. Overall, we believe that the AG sampler’s ease of implementation and competitive performance make it an excellent method to sample from Potts models.

Our paper also provides bounds on the mixing time of AG samplers. Such bounds exist for the Heat Bath and Swendsen-Wang algorithms. To the best of our knowledge, our paper provides the first bounds for AG samplers. Our bounds are of similar order as those for Swendsen-Wang algorithms (see, e.g., Galanis et al. (2019)).

There exist several directions for future research. First, it would be of interest to establish matching lower bounds on the mixing time for Theorems 5 and 9. Second, it would be interesting to extend Theorem 9 to the low-temperature regime for broader classes of models, such as Potts models on random regular graphs. Another direction for future research is to investigate other algorithms which use the auxiliary Gaussian variables we propose. This includes discrete HMC (Zhang et al., 2012) and more generally gradient-based methods to sample over 𝐙\bf Z. An important challenge here is to understand the geometry of p⁡(𝐙)p({\bf Z}) and which methods—or which tuning of a method—enable efficient sampling. Similarly, it is of interest to study how tempering best works with an AG sampler, or any sampler over ℙ⁡(𝐗,𝐙)\mathbb{P}({\bf X},{\bf Z}) in order to sample from cold systems.

Appendix

The Appendix contains proofs missing in the main body. We derive the conditional and marginal distributions, that arise when we introduce either a regular or low-rank auxiliary Gaussian variable for Potts models. We prove Proposition 3, which characterizes the error committed in using the low-rank algorithm, and Proposition 4, which characterizes the type of coupling matrices for which we may want to use a low-rank algorithm. Specialized algorithms for the Ising model (q=2q=2) are derived. We also provide an overview on auxiliary cluster and tempering algorithms.

The code used for our numerical experiments can be found at https://github.com/charlesm93/potts_simulation. The ReadMe provides instructions on how to run the code.

Appendix C Specialized Auxiliary Gaussian algorithm for q=2q=2

C.1 Standard Auxiliary Gaussian algorithm

Setting 𝐖:=𝐙1−𝐙2\mathbf{W}:=\mathbf{Z}_{1}-\mathbf{Z}_{2} and using (5), under ℙ\mathbb{P} we have

(𝐖|𝐗=𝐱)∼N⁡(𝐲1−𝐲2,2​B−1).\displaystyle(\mathbf{W}|\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x})\sim N(\mathbf{y}_{1}-\mathbf{y}_{2},2B^{-1}). (73)

Also, using (6), we have

ℙ⁡(Xi=1|𝐙=𝐳)=\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(X_{i}=1|\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{z})= exp⁡(∑j=1nBi​j​z1​j)exp⁡(∑j=1nBi​j​z1​j)+exp⁡(∑j=1nBi​j​z2​j)\displaystyle\frac{\exp\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}z_{1j}\Big)}{\exp\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}z_{1j}\Big)+\exp\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}z_{2j}\Big)}
=\displaystyle= exp⁡(12​∑j=1nBi​j​wj)exp(12∑j=1nBi​jwj)+exp(−12∑j=1nBi​jwj),\displaystyle\frac{\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}w_{j}\Big)}{\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}w_{j}\Big)+\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}w_{j}\Big)}, (74)

where wj=z1​j−z2​jw_{j}=z_{1j}-z_{2j}. A similar calculation gives

ℙ⁡(Xi=2|𝐙=𝐳)=exp(−12∑j=1nBi​jwj)exp(12∑j=1nBi​jwj)+exp(−12∑j=1nBi​jwj).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(X_{i}=2|\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{z})=\frac{\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}w_{j}\Big)}{\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}w_{j}\Big)+\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}w_{j}\Big)}.

Thus, instead of using the 2​n2n dimensional Gaussian 𝐙{\mathbf{Z}}, one can use the nn dimensional Gaussian WW, and iterate between (73) and (74), This is the same exact algorithm, but we work with a lower dimensional representation of the auxiliary variable, which helps in faster computations. We note that this is the exact same algorithm as (Martens and Sutskever, 2010) in the Ising case.

C.2 Low rank Auxiliary Gaussian algorithm

Setting 𝐖:=𝐙1−𝐙2\mathbf{W}:=\mathbf{Z}_{1}-\mathbf{Z}_{2} as before, using (13) under ℚ\mathbb{Q} we have

(𝐖j|𝐗=𝐱)∼N⁡(𝐩j′​(𝐲1−𝐲2),2/μj),\displaystyle(\mathbf{W}_{j}|\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x})\sim N(\mathbf{p}_{j}^{\prime}(\mathbf{y}_{1}-\mathbf{y}_{2}),2/\mu_{j}), (75)

with (W1,…,Wk)(W_{1},\ldots,W_{k}) mutually independent. Also, using (14), we have

ℚ⁡(Xi=1|𝐙=𝐳)=\displaystyle\mathbb{Q}(X_{i}=1|\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{z})= exp⁡(∑j=1kμj​z1​j​pj​i)exp⁡(∑j=1kμj​z1​j​pj​i)+exp⁡(∑j=1kμj​z2​j​pj​i)\displaystyle\frac{\exp\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}z_{1j}p_{ji}\Big)}{\exp\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}z_{1j}p_{ji}\Big)+\exp\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}z_{2j}p_{ji}\Big)}
=\displaystyle= exp⁡(12​∑j=1kμj​wj​pj​i)exp(12∑j=1kμjwjpj​i)+exp(−12∑j=1kμjwjpj​i),\displaystyle\frac{\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}w_{j}p_{ji}\Big)}{\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}w_{j}p_{ji}\Big)+\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}w_{j}p_{ji}\Big)}, (76)

where wj=z1​j−z2​jw_{j}=z_{1j}-z_{2j}. A similar calculation gives

ℚ⁡(Xi=2|𝐙=𝐳)=exp(−12∑j=1kμjwjpj​i)exp(12∑j=1kμjwjpj​i)+exp(−12∑j=1kμjwjpj​i).\displaystyle\mathbb{Q}(X_{i}=2|\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{z})=\frac{\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}w_{j}p_{ji}\Big)}{\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}w_{j}p_{ji}\Big)+\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}w_{j}p_{ji}\Big)}.

Thus, instead of using the 2​k2k dimensional Gaussian 𝐙{\mathbf{Z}}, one can use the kk dimensional Gaussian WW, and iterate between (75) and (76).

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
